jobs.description: Onyx Security Series B: Keeping Humans in Control | Onyx Blog Update cookies preferences Read More: Onyx Security Announces $113M Series B Funding Round Platform Platform Overview Observability Security Governance Orchestration ROI Integration Partners Anthropic Open AI Amazon Microsoft Google Solutions Agent Identity and Access Governance AI Discovery and Shadow AI MCP Security Runtime and Prompt Injection Defense Integrations Anthropic Open AI Amazon Microsoft Google Resources Events Blog Glossary Company About Newsroom Careers Trust Center Control AI, Create The Impossible Get a demo Get a demo ONYX Blog Onyx’s $113M Series B: Keeping Humans in Control as AI Becomes Smarter Maxim Bar Kogan , CEO & Co-Founder | Read time : 3 mins Published : 29 Jul 2026 | Updated : August 7, 2026 Share When we started Onyx, the question I could not stop thinking about was this: when something smarter than you is responsible for the things you depend on, how do you stay in control? Two years later, that question is no longer hypothetical. A year ago, almost nothing inside the enterprise was done by an agent. A year from now, most actions inside the enterprise will be. And not long after that, entire companies will run as autonomous agent operations, making the decisions humans used to make about capital allocation, energy grids, patient care, and supply chains. The models underneath those agents are crossing into the realm of general intelligence. Their capability at this level makes AI a national security matter, and it is arriving faster than the controls around it. The gap between what advanced AI can do and what humans can govern is widening, not narrowing. The upside is real: abundance, resilient supply of food and energy. The risk is that we delegate those decisions to systems no one is watching, on infrastructure no one is governing. Humans need to stay in control of advanced AI. Not by holding it back. By governing it well enough to safely let it further into the fabric of how we run critical industries. That is why we built the Secure AI Control Plane. And that is why, today, I am announcing that Onyx has raised $113 million in Series B funding led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Cyberstarts, TCV, Conviction, FirstMark, Vintage Investment Partners, QuantumLight, and G Squared. What the round is for The Series B is not about market share inside a category that already exists. It is about building the platform that lets humans stay in control as agents take on more of the work. Every enterprise is becoming an agent operator, whether they planned to or not. Agents now operate across the browser, endpoint, SaaS, and cloud surfaces where enterprises are standing up their AI programs. The Secure AI Control Plane governs the agent where the actor lives. It discovers the AI agents in the environment and inspects every action before it takes effect, without slowing adoption down. Onyx already secures more than 1.1 million agents across our enterprise customers and inspects more than 66 million AI sessions in real time. That footprint is what makes the control problem tractable, not hypothetical. Where this work is most urgent The industries that carry the weight of critical infrastructure need this first. Energy, financial services, healthcare. These are the sectors where an agent making the wrong decision at production speed does not produce a headline; it produces an outage, a market event, or a life at risk. The Fortune 500 companies we work with across these industries are the ones setting the pace on how agent governance actually gets deployed. The depth we owe them is the reason for the Series B. I want to thank our customers for trusting Onyx with the AI programs, our investors, and the entire team at Onyx who helped turn conviction into a control plane a CISO can actually deploy inside their business, on the timeline the business needs. The question I started with is still the question I am working on. When something smarter than you is responsible for the things you depend on, how do you stay in control? We are answering it. And we are moving quickly, because advanced AI is not slowing down for the security controls around it to catch up. Frequently Asked Questions What is the Secure AI Control Plane from Onyx? The Secure AI Control Plane is Onyx Security's platform for governing enterprise AI agents across browser, endpoint, SaaS, and cloud surfaces. It discovers AI agents in an environment and inspects every action before it takes effect – without slowing adoption. Onyx currently secures more than 1.1 million agents and inspects over 66 million AI sessions in real time. How does agent governance differ from traditional AI security? Traditional AI security focuses on protecting models and data at rest. Agent governance operates at runtime, inspecting every prompt, response, and agent action as it happens across production environments. This runtime approach addresses the control gap created when autonomous agents make decisions at production speed in critical industries like energy, healthcare, and financial services. How does Onyx inspect AI agent actions at runtime? Onyx governs AI agents where the actor lives – across browser, endpoint, SaaS, and cloud surfaces. The platform discovers agents operating in the environment and inspects each action before it takes effect. This runtime inspection covers every prompt, response, and agent action, enforcing controls without introducing friction that slows enterprise AI adoption. What business risks does enterprise AI agent governance reduce? Without agent governance, autonomous AI agents making decisions at production speed in critical infrastructure sectors can cause outages, market events, or endanger lives. The Onyx Security Series B funding of $113 million reflects growing enterprise demand for controls that let organizations safely scale AI adoption while maintaining human oversight across capital allocation, energy grids

An agent reads a document, calls several APIs, and completes a task that used to require human action. Your SIEM was built for events, your DLP was built for files, neither one sees the agent decide what to do next. The answer is not to block AI with legacy tools, but to make safe AI adoption possible by protecting agents at run-time. The Onyx Difference Inline Inspection Across Every AI Surface Onyx inspects every prompt, tool call, and model response inline across browser AI, coding assistants, desktop AI agents, cloud workloads, and MCP servers. Five enforcement actions: alert, block, mask, steer, or ask (human in-the-loop). Coverage extends across the AI surfaces enterprises actually run, all under one policy. Posture Management for the Agent Lifecycle Every agent is evaluated on deployment and continuously across its lifecycle. Misconfigurations, excessive permissions, credential handling, and blast radius roll into one risk view that stays current as the agent changes, giving security architects a single defensible posture score for release sign-off. Autonomous Agentic Red Teaming Red teaming continuously attacks deployed agents to surface what static reviews miss, generating attack plans across reconnaissance, jailbreaking, and weaponization. Findings feed the same platform your team uses for runtime enforcement, keeping test and production on one policy record instead of two disconnected tools. See Onyx Connect to Your Stack Onyx drops in next to the identity, cloud, network, and endpoint tools your team already runs. Most environments produce a working AI inventory within 24 hours and an enforced governance policy on day one. To see real-time AI security across your stack... schedule a demo Connects to the Tools You Already Run Onyx fits into the security stack your team already runs, so enforcement stays in context and investigations stay in workflow. Policy decisions align with identity and endpoint context from the systems your team already uses. Alerts and full session records synchronize with your SIEM, so analysts can trace an incident end-to-end without leaving the tool. Coverage extends across browser AI, coding agents, cloud workloads, MCP servers, and the agent-building platforms in use today, all under the same policy. Frequently Asked Questions What is Onyx AI Security? The runtime and posture layer of the Onyx Secure AI Control Plane. One platform discovers AI agents across your environment, scores their runtime posture, and enforces policy on every agent action and every MCP call. How is this different from existing detection tools? Existing detection observes the action after it happens and writes an alert. Onyx intervenes at the moment an action would execute, so an unauthorized step is blocked, masked, or redirected instead of just logged. The difference between observing an exfiltration and preventing it is the difference between an audit log and a control. How does Onyx integrate with my existing stack? Onyx pulls identity context from Okta and Microsoft Entra, and endpoint management context from Intune, Jamf, and Tanium. Alerts and session records forward to Splunk and CrowdStrike NG-SIEM. No SDK changes required for application teams. Is Onyx certified? SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified, with compliance mapping for OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, and ISO 42001. Onyx compiles it into runtime enforcement and applies it across every current and future agent in scope, and across the MCP servers those agents reach. The Onyx Difference Designed for the Agent Identity When multiple users delegate to the same agent across tools, Onyx gives that agent its own identity, separate from the invoker. Govern, audit, and control one agent actor with one line of accountability, instead of reconciling scattered audit trails that only make sense one credential at a time. When a new tool or server is detected, Onyx finds it, scores it for risk, and routes the approval decision before any agent uses it, keeping the trusted set current as the tool landscape grows. Violations and their session records synchronize with your SIEM, keeping compliance evidence and audit response in the tools your security and GRC teams already use. Framework mappings for OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, and ISO 42001 are applied automatically, so audit and regulator responses draw from the same policy record. Frequently Asked Questions How does natural-language policy work? You write the intent in plain English. Onyx compiles it into enforcement logic, applies it across every agent in scope, and logs every decision with a traceable record back to the original statement. Which compliance frameworks does Onyx cover? OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, and ISO 42001. How is per-agent identity governance different from standard IAM? Standard IAM governs humans and service accounts. AI agents are neither. Each governed agent carries its own Onyx-attributed identity, distinct from the user who invoked it, and the same record tracks the per-tool-call and per-MCP-call identities the agent uses at each step. How is this different from DLP or SASE? DLP and SASE enforce at the network or file level. They were not built to inspect AI agent tool calls or apply policy logic the moment an action would execute. Onyx operates at the agent behavior layer and forwards alerts and sessions to your SIEM, extending your existing investigation surface rather than replacing it. Onyx discovers every Copilot Studio agent, governs each one under its own Entra ID identity, and scores connector exposure continuously. The Copilot Studio Security Challenge Copilot Studio has become the default place for business teams to build AI agents inside Microsoft. Finance teams ship agents that read invoices and update records. HR teams build agents that summarize policy and route requests. Operations teams connect agents to ticketing systems, knowledge bases, and external APIs through the Power Platform connector library. That maker velocity creates a new security challenge: business-built agents accumulate faster than IAM can keep up. Agents stand up outside the standard provisioning workflow. Connector permissions drift. Maker-scoped connectors grant access to the maker's data regardless of who invokes the agent. Purview handles data classification and Copilot Studio orchestrates agent building. Neither one tells the security architect which agent acted, under whose authority, against which Dataverse table or SharePoint site, at the moment the action lands. The ability to automatically discover, govern, and secure Copilot agents is vital for enterprises. Onyx makes it easy. Bringing Copilot Studio into Onyx's Secure AI Control Plane Onyx integrates with Microsoft Copilot Studio through the Microsoft Graph API. No proxies. No traffic rerouting. No SDK changes for the application teams or business users building agents. Setup uses a delegated or application connection scoped read-only against Copilot Studio agent telemetry. Every Copilot Studio agent in the tenant surfaces on day one, attributed to its Microsoft Entra ID identity (distinct from the user who invoked it), with its full configuration on one record: connectors, scope (maker or user), actions, topics, generative actions, owner, and lifecycle stage. Onyx enriches agent activity in near real time with the Dataverse table queried, the SharePoint site accessed, and the broader AI usage context from the rest of your enterprise. This feeds into the Onyx model engine, allowing Onyx to continuously assess agent posture, surface zombie agents with active data access and no owner, and alert on every risky configuration before the agent ships. The Benefits of Onyx + Microsoft Copilot Studio Observability See every Copilot Studio agent in the tenant, the Power Platform connectors it has been granted, the data classes it can reach, and what it has actually done. Governance Evaluate Copilot Studio agent activity against natural-language policies, alert on maker-scoped connector exposure, and create an audit trail mapped to OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, and ISO 42001. Security Posture Continuously assess every Copilot Studio agent for misconfigurations, maker-scope drift, and generative action prompt-injection susceptibility, with Agentic Red Teaming findings translating directly into runtime policy. Runtime Security Inspect every prompt, tool call, and Dataverse or SharePoint connector action inline, catch off-scope behavior the moment it would land, and steer the unsafe action toward a safe alternative without stopping the workflow. Govern Copilot Studio Without Slowing Down Business Teams Security teams should not have to block Copilot Studio adoption or slow down business-team agent deployment to reduce risk. Onyx lets teams define and enforce natural-language policies across the full Copilot Studio surface, helping protect sensitive Dataverse data, regulated information, and business-critical Power Platform workflows without slowing adoption. Purview governs the data layer. Copilot Studio orchestrates the agent building experience. Onyx is the agent control plane on top: discovery, identity governance, posture scoring, and runtime enforcement on every prompt, tool call, and connector action. Business users keep building agents; security teams keep the visibility and the controls needed to govern what gets shipped. To see the impact of real-time AI security with Onyx and Microsoft Copilot Studio, schedule a demo. Current Onyx customers can get started by following these simple integration steps. Adversarial machine learning The discipline of attacking and defending machine learning systems, with NIST AI 100-2 providing the canonical taxonomy security teams map coverage against. A Agentic AI The category term for the shift from AI that responds to AI that acts, describing a change in how AI is deployed rather than any particular architecture. A Agent identity A distinct, traceable identity for an AI agent, separate from the user who initiated it, recording its author, its credential type, and its downstream scope. A Agent sprawl AI agents accumulating faster than any process can register and govern them, driven by low-code builders, embedded SaaS features, and agents creating other agents. A AI agent A system that reasons about a goal, calls tools to act on it, and adapts to results, holding an identity, permissions, a reasoning loop, a tool catalog, and memory. A AI agent governance The policies and enforcement mechanisms determining which agents may exist and what they may do, spanning inventory, identity, permission, runtime policy, and audit. A AI asset tagging Attaching labels such as owner, environment, and risk level to discovered AI assets, turning a flat inventory of thousands into groups that policy can address. A AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) A structured inventory of every component inside an AI system, extending the software bill of materials concept to models, datasets, prompts, agents, and tool catalogs. A AI compliance Meeting the regulatory, standards-based, contractual, and internal obligations governing enterprise AI use, from inventory and risk assessment to incident reporting. A AI control plane The platform layer governing every agent, model, and MCP server in an enterprise, and the AI-layer analog to the control planes already running for cloud and identity. A AI discovery Continuous identification and inventory of every AI asset across an environment, read from several surfaces because no single signal source sees the whole footprint. A AI guardrails The controls defining what an AI system may accept, produce, and do at runtime, and the colloquial umbrella above the policy engine that actually enforces them. A AI hallucination Model output presented as factual but grounded in nothing, ranging from small factual drift up to fabricated citations, APIs, and wholly invented sources. A AI intervention The runtime control function that acts on an agent's action before it completes, and the third core function of an AI control plane after discovery and observation. A AI Observability Continuous, evidence-grade visibility into what AI agents, models, and MCP servers are and how they behave at runtime, spanning inventory through to behavioral baselining. A AI orchestration The layer routing and governing AI traffic across providers, MCP servers, and agents, covering LLM gateways, MCP gateways, and agent-level workflow composition. A AI policy engine The runtime component compiling authored governance rules into checks that intercept prompts and agent actions before they execute, beneath AI agent governance. A AI red teaming Adversarial probing of AI systems to find security, safety, and reliability failures before production, combining human creativity with automated agent-driven testing. A AI ROI Measurement of the business return on AI investment alongside its cost and risk, across four metric families: adoption, value, cost, and risk exposure. A AI runtime security The inline layer inspecting and controlling AI activity as it executes, narrower and more specific than LLM security, which spans the whole model lifecycle. A AI security posture management (AI-SPM) Continuous inventory, evaluation, and prioritized remediation for AI assets, extending cloud and SaaS posture management to agents, models, and AI applications. A AI TRiSM Gartner's category for AI trust, risk, and security management, spanning four pillars: explainability, ModelOps, AI application security, and model privacy. A EU AI Act The EU's horizontal AI regulation, classifying systems as unacceptable, high, limited, or minimal risk and placing obligations on both providers and deployers. E Human-in-the-loop An architectural pattern where an AI system pauses for human review before specified actions, gated selectively on action class, blast radius, or model confidence. H Just-in-time access (for agents) Granting an agent the permissions a specific request requires at the moment of the request, evaluated against live context and released rather than held standing. J LLM data leakage Sensitive information escaping through a model's outputs, training data, or tool calls, along direct, indirect, and structural paths conventional DLP was not written to see. L LLM jailbreaking Bypassing the safety training in a language model so it produces content it would normally refuse, through role-play framing, encoding, or multi-turn conditioning. L LLM observability The engineering discipline of instrumenting LLM applications for quality and cost, distinct from AI observability, which asks a security and governance question. Audit Logging Onyx systems that handle sensitive information, accept network connections, or manage access control record audit logs capturing what activity was performed, who performed it, when and how, and the result. Logged events include user authentication, all actions taken by administrators, and attempts to grant, modify, or revoke access rights. Multi-Factor Authentication Multi-factor authentication is required on every system that offers it. Access to Onyx systems and applications is controlled through unique user login IDs, with authentication requirements enforced consistently across all systems. Role-Based Access Control All access to Onyx systems and data is regulated through role-based access control, with the level of access based on the minimum necessary to carry out a user's job responsibilities. Segregation of duties is considered when user rights are assigned. Data Security How Onyx classifies, encrypts, backs up, and physically protects the data it holds. Data Asset Classification Data is classified at the time of creation or acquisition into one of three levels: Confidential/Restricted, Internal Use, or Public. The classification determines the baseline security controls, handling requirements, and retention that apply to that data. Data Backups Complete backups are performed daily and automatically replicated to a separate region within the same country. Backups are encrypted in the same way as live production data, and backup failures trigger an incident alert to the Security Officer. Encryption-at-rest Data encryption keys use AES-256 with 256-bit key sizes, as defined in Onyx's Encryption Policy. Backups are encrypted to the same standard as live production data. Encryption-in-transit Traffic to the Onyx platform is protected in transit using SSL/TLS certificates. Cryptographic controls follow the approved algorithms and key sizes defined in Onyx's Encryption Policy, and conform to international standards.
